commitResults.messageTitle: Rename chatbot from Duke to Rex; add greeting and exit message
commitResults.messageBody:
Renames the placeholder Duke.java to Rex.java, updates the ASCII
banner, and adds a greeting/farewell so the chatbot has an identity
and completes the Level-0 requirement. README and docs/README
updated to match the new name.

commitResults.messageTitle: Echo user input; exit on bye command
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds a Scanner-based input loop so Rex echoes back whatever the user
types, and exits with a farewell when the input is "bye". Completes
the Level-1 requirement.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add ability to store and list tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Any input other than "list" or "bye" is stored in memory (fixed-size
array, up to 100 tasks) and confirmed with "added: ...". The "list"
command prints all stored tasks, numbered. Completes the Level-2
requirement.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add present-changes-visually skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Project-specific Claude Code skill (adapted from
https://github.com/se-edu/skill-present-changes-visually) that
generates a self-contained HTML split-view diff between any two
points in the repo's history (commits, tags, branches, or the
current worktree). Useful for visually reviewing AI-generated
changes before committing, e.g. when comparing before/after a
refactor like the upcoming Task class extraction.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add mark command to update task status (no new classes yet)
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds a parallel boolean[] done array and a "mark <n>" command that
sets a task's done status, printing the confirmation with its status
icon. Also updates "list" to show the status icon and header line.
This is step 1 of Level-3 (mark before unmark, and before introducing
a Task class for the A-Classes extension), so no tag yet.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add unmark command to reverse task status
commitResults.messageBody:
Mirrors the mark command: "unmark <n>" sets a task's done status back
to false and confirms with its status icon. Step 2 of Level-3, still
before the Task class refactor for A-Classes, so no tag yet.

commitResults.messageTitle: Introduce Task class (A-Classes extension)
commitResults.messageBody:
Replaces the parallel String[] tasks / boolean[] done arrays with a
single Task[] array. Task bundles a task's description and done
status together, with markAsDone()/markAsNotDone()/getStatusIcon()
methods, so the two no longer need to be kept in sync by index.
Behavior is unchanged; verified via a before/after visual diff.
Completes the Level-3 requirement (mark/unmark + A-Classes).

commitResults.messageTitle: Add test-ui skill and console regression test plan
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds a project-specific Claude Code skill that runs the test cases in
test/ui-test-plan.md against the compiled program: one full console
session per test case, checking output after each input, stopping
immediately and reporting expected-vs-actual on the first mismatch.

Seeds test/ui-test-plan.md with regression coverage for current
behavior (greet/exit, add/list, mark/unmark).

Updates AGENTS.md so future code changes update the test plan (when
needed) and invoke the test-ui skill before being considered done.

commitResults.messageTitle: docs: adopt Conventional Commits for commit messages
commitResults.messageBody:
Records the convention in AGENTS.md so commit subject lines use a
type prefix (feat/fix/refactor/test/docs/chore) going forward.

commitResults.messageTitle: feat: add ToDo, Deadline, and Event task types (A-Inheritance)
commitResults.messageBody:
Refactors Task into a base class with overridable getTypeIcon() and
getDetails() hooks, and adds ToDo/Deadline/Event as subclasses. Wires
up three new commands in Rex.java:

- "todo <desc>"
- "deadline <desc> /by <string>"
- "event <desc> /from <string> /to <string>"

Retires the old plain-text add fallback from Level-2/3, since every
add now goes through one of the three type-specific commands (no
example in the spec uses bare-text add from this point on; Level-5
will add proper error handling for unrecognized input instead).

Updates the add-confirmation and list output formats to include the
type icon and per-type details (by/from-to), and updates
test/ui-test-plan.md to match. All test-ui cases pass. Completes the
Level-4 requirement.

commitResults.messageTitle: style: give Rex a playful dog personality
commitResults.messageBody:
Reworks the greeting, farewell, list header, and add/mark/unmark
confirmation messages to lean into "Rex" as a dog theme, per the
spec's encouragement to customize the chatbot's personality. Content
and format (task lines, counts, icons) are unchanged, so this is a
wording-only pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: feat: handle errors via RexException
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds RexException, a custom checked exception thrown for any bad
input, caught centrally in Rex.java's main loop and printed with an
"OOPS!!!" prefix. Covers every error currently possible:

- unrecognized commands
- empty description for todo/deadline/event
- deadline missing "/by", event missing "/from" or "/to"
- mark/unmark with a non-numeric, missing, or out-of-range task
  number (previously these crashed the program uncaught)

Each message is specific to the error rather than generic, and the
deadline/event messages include a corrected usage example. Completes
the Level-5 requirement.

commitResults.messageTitle: feat: add delete command; switch tasks to ArrayList
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds "delete <n>" to remove a task, reusing the same task-number
validation as mark/unmark. Replaces the fixed-size Task[100] array
and its manual taskCount bookkeeping with ArrayList<Task>, since
ArrayList.remove(index) handles the element-shifting that a manual
delete on a plain array would otherwise require, and removes the
artificial 100-task cap. Completes the Level-6 requirement.

commitResults.messageTitle: refactor: dispatch commands via CommandType enum (A-Enums)
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds a CommandType enum (LIST, MARK, UNMARK, DELETE, TODO, DEADLINE,
EVENT, BYE, UNKNOWN) and replaces the chain of input.equals/startsWith
checks in Rex.java's main loop with a switch on the parsed command
word. Makes the set of valid commands explicit in one place instead
of implicit across a string comparison chain. Pure refactor, no
behavior change (verified via visual diff and test-ui), aside from
command words now being matched case-insensitively as a side effect
of the uppercase lookup.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Record course coding and Git standards
commitResults.messageBody:
The course requires the SE-EDU Java and Git standards from Week 3
onward, and the A-CodingStandard increment is graded against them.
Recording them in AGENTS.md keeps the rules next to the code rather
than in a browser tab, so every later increment is written to the
standard instead of being retrofitted to it.

Also captures the branch, no-fast-forward merge, tag and push
sequence that each branched increment repeats.

commitResults.messageTitle: test-ui: Isolate each test case in a temp folder
commitResults.messageBody:
Test cases currently run with the repository root as their working
directory. Once the chatbot saves tasks to a file, every test case
would share one save file: tasks added by one case would be loaded
by the next, making the suite order-dependent, and running the
tests would overwrite real task data in the repository.

Run each test case in its own empty temporary directory instead, so
files a case writes are invisible to other cases and to the repo.

Also add a (restart) directive, which relaunches the program in the
same directory mid-case. Without it there is no way to express the
one behaviour the save feature exists to provide: that tasks added
in one session are still there in the next.

commitResults.messageTitle: Save tasks to data/rex.txt when the list changes
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks are lost when the program exits, so the same list has to be
retyped on every run.

Add a Storage class that writes the tasks to a file, and call it
after any command that changes the list. Storage is the only class
that knows where the tasks are kept or how the file is laid out, so
the rest of the program is unaffected by that choice. Its path is
built from separate name parts rather than a string with "/" in it,
so it resolves correctly on any operating system, and the enclosing
folder is created on demand for the common case of a first run.

Each task type writes its own line via toSaveFormat(), so adding a
task type later means adding one method rather than editing a
central writer that switches on the type.

A failed write warns and lets the session continue: the user's
tasks are still usable in memory, and ending the session over it
would throw away the very data the save was meant to protect.

Reading the file back is not implemented yet, so tasks written here
are not loaded on the next run.

commitResults.messageTitle: Load saved tasks on startup
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks were written to disk but never read back, so the file had no
effect and the list still started empty on every run.

Read the file when the program starts, rebuilding each task from its
line. Reading cannot be delegated to the task classes the way writing
is: there is no task object to ask yet, so Storage examines the type
letter to decide which kind of task to create.

A missing file is treated as an empty list rather than an error,
since that is the normal state on a first run and on any machine the
program has just been copied to. An unreadable file warns and starts
empty instead of refusing to launch, which would leave the user
unable to use the program at all.

The load runs between the two greeting lines so that anything it
reports appears before the user is invited to type a command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Skip unreadable lines in the save file
commitResults.messageBody:
A save file can be damaged: hand-edited, written by an older version
of the program, or left half-written by a crash. Parsing such a line
would have thrown an out-of-bounds error and stopped the program
before the user could reach any of their tasks.

Check every field of a line before using it, and treat a line that
fails as skippable rather than fatal. One unreadable line then costs
the user that line alone instead of every task in the file.

Report the total once at startup rather than per line, so a badly
damaged file does not bury the greeting under a wall of errors. The
skipped lines are not recovered: the next save rewrites the whole
file, and that warning is the user's only chance to intervene.

Add a (write) directive to the test plan, so a test case can put a
file on disk for the program to read. Without it there is no way to
test a damaged file, since each test case starts in an empty folder.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
Store a deadline's date as a date, not text
commitResults.messageBody:
A deadline's /by was kept as whatever text the user typed, so the
program could not tell "2019-10-15" from "Sunday", and had no way to
answer any question about when a task actually falls.

Add TaskDateTime, which reads yyyy-mm-dd with an optional 24-hour time
and remembers whether a time was given, so a whole-day deadline is not
forced to invent one. It shows a date as Oct 15 2019 but writes the
format it reads, so a saved date survives a restart unchanged. Its
formatters are pinned to one locale, because an unpinned formatter
follows the machine's own and would print 6:00pm here but 6:00PM in
the United States.

An unreadable date is reported as an IllegalArgumentException: Storage
already skips a save-file line for that, and Rex turns it into a
RexException so a mistyped date reads as an ordinary error and the
session carries on.

Events keep their free-text /from and /to for now.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store an event's dates as dates, not text
commitResults.messageBody:
An event's /from and /to were still free text after the previous
commit, which left the two task types inconsistent and kept events out
of any question asked about when a task falls.

Give both ends a TaskDateTime, the same as a deadline's /by. Because
the time is optional at each end independently, a meeting can run from
2019-10-15 1400 to 1600 while a retreat simply spans 2019-10-18 to
2019-10-20 with no times at all.

The examples in the '/from' and '/to' error messages are updated to
show the format the program now accepts.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add an 'on' command to list a day's tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Storing dates as dates was only worth doing if something then asks
questions of them, and nothing did: a date could be typed, saved and
printed back, but never searched.

Add 'on <date>', which lists the tasks falling on one day. A deadline
falls on the day it is due whatever time it carries, and an event falls
on every day it spans, both ends included, so a retreat running from
the 18th to the 20th is found on the 19th. Each task answers for
itself through Task.isOn, which a plain todo inherits as false, so a
new kind of task decides the question rather than the search having to
learn about it.

Matches keep their number from the full list instead of being
renumbered from 1, so a number seen here still names the same task to
mark, unmark or delete.

The command takes a whole day and refuses a time of day, because
quietly dropping the time would hide that it was never used.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
Extract a Ui class for all console input and output
commitResults.messageBody:
Rex did everything: it read the keyboard, worked out what each command
meant, and formatted every line it printed. Changing the wording of a
message meant editing the middle of the command loop, where the logic
lives.

Move the Scanner and every System.out.println into Ui, which becomes
the only class that touches the console. Rex now asks for what it
wants shown -- ui.showAdded(task, count), ui.showError(message) -- and
no longer knows how a task is laid out on a line.

The program's output is unchanged; this moves code without altering
behaviour.

Choosing which tasks fall on a given day still happens inside
showTasksOn, which is not really a Ui concern. Extracting TaskList
next gives it a better home.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a TaskList class to hold the tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Rex passed a bare ArrayList<Task> around, so anything wanting to ask a
question about the list as a whole had to work the answer out for
itself. That is how choosing the tasks on a given day ended up inside
Ui, where deciding what to show is not the job.

Add TaskList, which owns the list and answers questions about it: add,
delete, get, size, and findIndicesOn for the on command. Ui is now
handed the positions to show rather than working them out, so it only
renders.

findIndicesOn returns positions rather than the matching tasks
themselves, because the user identifies a task by its number in the
whole list, and that number is lost the moment the matches are handed
back on their own.

The program's output is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop TaskList handing out its own list
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList held its ArrayList privately but then returned it from
getTasks, so any caller could clear the list, or add a null to it,
without going through the class at all. Holding the list privately
bought nothing while the getter gave it away.

Return an unmodifiable view instead. Saving reads it exactly as
before; attempting to change it now fails at run time.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser class: extract command reading from Rex
commitResults.messageBody:
Rex knows the shape of every command: that a deadline's date follows
"/by", that an event's times are split by "/from" and "/to", and what
to say when any of that is missing.

That knowledge sits inside the loop that dispatches commands, so the
loop reads as text handling rather than as what each command does, and
teaching Rex a new command word means editing the loop itself.

Let's move it into a Parser class that turns raw text into checked
values: a CommandType, a task number, a day, or the ToDo, Deadline or
Event that a line describes.

Parsing gets its own class rather than a set of helpers on Rex because
it is a whole responsibility, not a detail of running the loop. The
rest of the program can then work with tasks and numbers instead of
with strings.

Rex drops from 220 lines to 119. The program's output is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Record the commit body structure
commitResults.messageBody:
The Git section asks for a body explaining what changed and why, which
is a loose paraphrase of the SE-EDU standard.

The standard prescribes a five-part structure and two rules the
paraphrase leaves out: the current situation is written in the present
tense, and words like "currently" or "still" are omitted because
describing the situation implies them. Following the paraphrase
produces bodies that read as past-tense narration instead.

Let's record the template and both rules in full.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rex class: run the chatbot as an object
commitResults.messageBody:
Rex is a single static main method that keeps the Ui, the Storage and
the task list as local variables, with the command switch written
inline in the loop that reads input.

Every helper has to be handed whatever it needs as an argument, and
one method greets the user, dispatches each command and decides when
to save.

Let's make the three parts fields, give the class a constructor and a
run method, and move the command switch into a private execute method.

Loading stays in run rather than the constructor, unlike the shape the
brief sketches, because a load reports unreadable lines to the user
and those have to appear after the greeting rather than before it. A
constructor that prints is worse than one that only wires things up.

The three commands that add a task now share an addTask helper. The
program's output is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: TaskList class: check task numbers in the list itself
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser both reads a task number and checks that a task has it, which
it can only do because Rex hands it the current task count.

Extracting Command classes will leave Parser with no task list to ask,
since a command is built from the input alone, before anything looks
at the tasks.

Let's give TaskList getByNumber and deleteByNumber, which refuse a
number that names no task, and leave Parser deciding only whether the
argument is a number at all.

The check belongs with the list in any case: whether a number names a
task depends on how many there are, which is the list's own business.

Marking a task no longer looks it up twice, once to change it and once
to show it. The program's output is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Command classes: replace the dispatch switch
commitResults.messageBody:
Rex.execute is a switch over CommandType with a branch per command, so
Rex holds both the loop and the knowledge of what every command does.

Adding a command means editing that switch, and what a command needs
-- a task, a number, a day -- is unpacked into local variables inside
its branch instead of belonging to anything.

Let's give each command a class: an abstract Command with execute,
isExit and isTaskListChanged, and nine subclasses that hold what they
need and carry themselves out. Parser.parse builds one, and Rex.run
runs whatever it is handed.

execute takes the task list and the Ui but not the Storage that the
brief's sketch passes in, so the message shown when a save fails stays
in one place rather than being repeated in every command that changes
something. Refusing an unrecognized word is itself a command, so the
loop always has something to run.

CommandType now names command words and nothing more. Rex drops from
153 lines to 94; the switch that remains is in Parser, choosing what
to build, and runs once per line rather than once per action. The
program's output is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreOOP'
Task class: offer the description through a getter
commitResults.messageBody:
Ui builds the line it shows by reading task.description directly, a
protected field it can reach only because every class sits in one
package.

Moving Task into a package of its own puts that field out of reach:
protected means subclasses and the same package, and Ui is neither.

Let's add getDescription and have Ui ask for it.

Widening the field to public would compile too, but a field anyone can
assign to is a worse trade than a method that only reads it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organize the classes into packages under rex
commitResults.messageBody:
All 21 classes sit directly in src/main/java with no package
declaration, so the source root doubles as the only namespace.

Nothing in the layout says which classes belong together, even though
A-MoreOOP grouped them by responsibility: a command class and a task
class sit side by side in one folder of 21 files.

Let's put everything under rex -- the components Ui, Parser, Storage
and TaskList alongside Rex and RexException, the Command hierarchy and
CommandType in rex.command, and the Task hierarchy with TaskDateTime
in rex.task.

src/main/java stays the source root, which the brief requires because
tools used in later increments look for the sources there. The split
follows what the classes are, and only the two groups big enough to
earn a folder get one.

This leaves a cycle between packages: rex.command reaches into rex for
Ui and TaskList, while rex reaches back through Parser to build the
commands. Java permits it, and it is the price of grouping by kind.

The files are moved with git mv so the history follows them. The
program's output is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: README.md: Point setup at the moved Rex.java
commitResults.messageBody:
The setup instructions tell the reader to open src/main/java/Rex.java
and run its main method.

That path no longer exists: Rex.java now sits in the rex package, so
anyone following the instructions on a fresh clone looks for a file
that is not there.

Let's give the path the class moved to.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Packages'
Add Gradle wrapper files
commitResults.messageBody:
Rex is built by invoking javac and java by hand, or through a run
configuration set up inside the IDE. Both have to be recreated on every
machine, neither can fetch third-party libraries, and neither produces a
distributable JAR.

Let's merge the add-gradle-support branch, which supplies a build.gradle
along with the Gradle wrapper.

The wrapper is a checked-in script that downloads the exact Gradle
version named in gradle-wrapper.properties, so anyone building the
project uses the same version without installing Gradle themselves.

The build.gradle that arrives still names the template's own entry point
and JAR name, which the next commit corrects.

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Point Gradle at Rex
commitResults.messageBody:
The build.gradle merged from the template names seedu.duke.Duke as the
application's entry point and duke.jar as the name of the fat JAR built
by shadowJar. Neither name exists in this project, so gradlew run fails
outright and any JAR produced is misnamed.

Let's set mainClass to rex.Rex and archiveFileName to rex.jar.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Gradle'
Add JUnit tests for reading dates
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing checks TaskDateTime automatically. Its behavior is confirmed by
running the chatbot and reading the output, so a date that stops parsing,
or a format that starts printing differently, is noticed only if someone
happens to look at the right line.

Let's test parse() and the two formats it feeds, covering dates with and
without a time, the malformed input each has to refuse, and a saved date
that is read back and compared against the original.

The display assertions spell out "Oct 15 2019, 6:00PM" in full. That is
what holds the formatters to one locale: unpinned, they print "6:00pm" on
this machine and the test fails.

Test methods are package-private, as JUnit does not need them public and
their names already say what each one checks.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for reading commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser turns everything the user types into tasks and numbers, and every
way of getting a command wrong has to arrive as a RexException carrying a
sentence fit to show. That is a lot of behavior resting on the console
tests alone.

Let's test parseDeadline, parseEvent and parseTaskNumber, covering the
well-formed forms, each part that can be left out or left empty, and the
dates that cannot be read.

Two of them compare the message and not only the exception type. A
deadline written with "/by" and nothing after it splits into an empty
date, so it is refused either way; only the message distinguishes a
missing date from an unreadable one.

Parsed tasks are compared through their save format, a single string
carrying the description, the done flag and every date the task holds.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JUnit'
Add Javadoc to the remaining classes and methods
commitResults.messageBody:
Task and ToDo carry no header comment at all, and twenty-five non-private
methods across the task and command classes go undocumented. The rules a
subclass is expected to follow, such as what a type icon is for, live only
in the code that happens to use them.

Let's document every non-private class and method that lacks a comment,
saying for each override what that one implementation does rather than
repeating the contract it inherits.

Warnings from javadoc -Xdoclint remain, and are left alone on purpose. They
ask for an @return on methods whose summary already gives the return value,
for a comment on each self-naming enum constant, and for an explicit
constructor on Command to hang a comment from. The coding standard this
project follows permits all three.

commitResults.messageTitle: Tighten field access and tidy two blank lines
commitResults.messageBody:
Five fields across the task classes are protected. Protected means this
class, its subclasses, and anything else in the same package, which is
wider than any of them needs: no subclass reads them, and a task's
description is already offered through a getter. Two methods additionally
open with a blank line, separating a body from its own signature.

Let's make the five fields private, marking the three that are never
reassigned final as well, and close the two gaps.

Task.getDescription carries a comment explaining why the field is
protected, so it is rewritten rather than left describing code that is no
longer there.

That everything still compiles is what shows the subclasses were not
reaching for those fields: any that did would stop resolving the moment
the field turned private.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-9: Add a find command
commitResults.messageBody:
Rex can only show every task at once, or the tasks falling on one day. A
list long enough to be worth keeping is one that has to be searched, and
there is no way to ask for a task by what it says.

Let's add find, which shows the tasks whose description contains a
keyword.

Matching ignores case and looks at any part of a description rather than
whole words, so "book" finds "bookshop" as well as "read book". The
keyword is taken whole instead of split, so "find return book" looks for
that phrase and not for either word on its own.

Matches keep the number they have in the full list rather than being
renumbered from 1. A renumbered list would show a task as 1 that mark and
delete know as something else, so acting on what was just found would hit
the wrong task. This follows what the on command already does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JavaDoc'
Merge branch 'branch-A-CodingStandard'
Merge branch 'branch-Level-9'
Level-10: Add JavaFX to the Gradle build
commitResults.messageBody:
Rex builds and runs as a console program, and its Gradle build knows
only about JUnit.

Level 10 adds a graphical interface, which needs the JavaFX libraries on
the compile and runtime classpath before any of that code can be
written.

Let's declare the JavaFX dependencies and point the application plugin
at a launcher class.

Each artifact is declared once per platform rather than letting Gradle
resolve only the current one, so that the shaded JAR runs on Windows,
macOS and Linux instead of only on the machine that built it. The entry
point is a separate Launcher because launching a class that extends
Application directly fails when JavaFX comes from the classpath, which
is how the JAR ships it.

That launcher does not exist yet, so ./gradlew run will not work until
the GUI code lands.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-10: Add a GUI using JavaFX
commitResults.messageBody:
Rex talks to the user through the console, and Ui prints each message to
System.out as it is produced.

Level 10 asks for a graphical interface. A window shows a whole reply at
once rather than a line at a time, and it cannot show what has already
gone to standard output, so the messages have to be obtainable as text.

Let's add a JavaFX front end, and teach Ui to collect its output instead
of printing it when asked.

Collecting inside Ui keeps the change small: every message already went
through that one class, so the eight Command classes are untouched and
still report through the same show methods. It also leaves the console
UI working, which is worth keeping because the core logic is far easier
to test through text than through a window.

The picture standing in for Rex is the one from the JavaFX tutorial, and
is meant to be replaced.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-10'
A-CheckStyle: Check the coding standard automatically
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing checks Rex against the coding standard except a person reading
the code, and a person reading the code misses things. Switch statements
across two classes indent their case labels level with the switch, which
the standard's own examples do not.

Rules that are read but never enforced drift, and the ones that go
unnoticed are the small layout rules that are tedious to check by eye
and easy to get wrong consistently.

Let's add Checkstyle to the build, with the configuration from
AddressBook Level 3, and fix what it reports.

The configuration is taken from AddressBook Level 3 rather than written
here, because it is the one the course provides as matching the required
standard, and a hand-written one would encode this project's habits
instead of the standard. Its version is pinned to the version that
project uses, so the file is read by the tool it was written for.

The 49 reported violations fell into three rules: case labels indented
level with their switch, missing separation between import groups, and
six wrapped lambda arguments that fit on one line anyway.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CheckStyle'
A-Varargs: Show grouped messages in one call
commitResults.messageBody:
Ui writes every line of a message with its own call to show(), so the
three lines confirming an added task are three consecutive statements.
Rex and Storage already accept a varargs path to their save file.

Three statements that must be shown together look no different from
three that merely sit next to each other, so nothing in the source says
the group is a group, and a line added to the middle of one reads as
unrelated.

Let's let show() take a variable number of lines.

Varargs suits this better than passing a list, because the lines are
written out at the call site rather than collected from anywhere, and a
list would add brackets around something that reads as ordinary
arguments. The lines still go out one at a time, so what the user sees
does not change.
